meta.titre: Complex Ions: Ligands, Coordination Number and Naming
meta.sous_theme: Ligands, coordination number and ligand exchange

sections.contenu_markdown: A cocoa farmer near Ebolowa dissolves a few crystals of bluestone, hydrated copper(II) sulfate, in water to spray his trees against black pod disease. The solution is a pale blue. When he spills a little ammonia solution from the cleaning bucket into it, the colour suddenly deepens to a rich dark blue. Both colours belong to complex ions, species in which a metal ion is surrounded by ligands. Every GCE Advanced Level Chemistry paper asks you to find the coordination number, the oxidation state, the name or the colour change of such a complex, so the rules are worth mastering.

items: Transition metals form ions with partly filled d orbitals, for example Cu2+ and Fe3+.
In a dative covalent bond both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom.
In a neutral compound the oxidation states add up to zero; in an ion they add up to the charge on the ion.
A lone pair is a pair of outer electrons not used in bonding, as on the nitrogen atom of NH3 and the oxygen atom of H2O.

sections.titre: Ligands, coordination number, oxidation state and naming
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **complex ion** is formed when a central metal ion is bonded to a number of **ligands** by dative covalent bonds. A ligand is a molecule or an ion with at least one lone pair of electrons that it donates to the metal ion. The metal ion must have low-lying empty orbitals (3d, 4s and 4p in the first transition series) in which to accept these pairs. A charge of +2 or more is not compulsory: $[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^{+}$ is a stable complex of a +1 ion.

| Ligand | Formula | Charge | Name in a complex | Donor atoms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Water | $\mathrm{H_2O}$ | 0 | aqua | 1 (monodentate) |
| Ammonia | $\mathrm{NH_3}$ | 0 | ammine | 1 (monodentate) |
| Chloride | $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ | -1 | chlorido (older texts: chloro) | 1 (monodentate) |
| Hydroxide | $\mathrm{OH^-}$ | -1 | hydroxido (hydroxo) | 1 (monodentate) |
| Cyanide | $\mathrm{CN^-}$ | -1 | cyanido (cyano) | 1 (monodentate) |
| Ethane-1,2-diamine | $\mathrm{NH_2CH_2CH_2NH_2}$ (en) | 0 | ethane-1,2-diamine | 2 (bidentate) |
| Ethanedioate (oxalate) | $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$ | -2 | ethanedioato (oxalato) | 2 (bidentate) |

**Coordination number** = the number of dative bonds from ligands to the metal ion, that is, the number of donor atoms, not the number of ligands.

**Charge on the complex** = oxidation state of the metal + the sum of the charges of the ligands. Use it in either direction: from the formula and the charge you can find the oxidation state of the metal.

**Shapes.** Coordination number 6 gives an octahedral complex, for example $[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$; coordination number 4 gives a tetrahedral complex such as $[\mathrm{CuCl_4}]^{2-}$ (some are square planar); coordination number 2 gives a linear complex such as $[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^{+}$.

**Naming rules.**
1. Name the ligands first, in alphabetical order of the ligand names (the prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- are ignored when ordering).
2. Show the number of each ligand with di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa; use bis, tris before names that are already complicated, such as ethane-1,2-diamine.
3. Then give the metal, followed by its oxidation state in Roman numerals in brackets.
4. If the complex is an anion the metal name ends in -ate (ferrate, cuprate, cobaltate); a cation or neutral complex keeps the ordinary name of the metal.

Examples: $[\mathrm{Cu(OH)_2(H_2O)_4}]$ is tetraaquadihydroxidocopper(II); $[\mathrm{CuCl_4}]^{2-}$ is tetrachloridocuprate(II) ion.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a ligand has more than one atom with a lone pair, or when you must explain why a chelate complex is unusually stable.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Ethane-1,2-diamine (en) has two nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair, so one molecule forms two dative bonds and closes a ring with the metal ion. In $[\mathrm{Ni(en)_3}]^{2+}$ there are three ligands but the coordination number is $3 \times 2 = 6$. EDTA$^{4-}$ is hexadentate: two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms bond to one metal ion, so one EDTA ion wraps completely around it.

Complexes with such **chelating** ligands are more stable than those with the same number of monodentate ligands. Compare the exchange $[\mathrm{Ni(H_{2}O)_{6}}]^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 3\mathrm{en}\mathrm{(aq)} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Ni(en)_3}]^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 6\mathrm{H_{2}O}\mathrm{(l)}$ One particle of complex and three of en replace four particles on the left by seven on the right, so the disorder (entropy) of the system increases and the reaction goes almost to completion even though the bond strengths are similar.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes a colour change on adding ammonia, concentrated hydrochloric acid or another ligand to a solution of a transition metal ion.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
In a ligand exchange reaction one ligand is replaced by another. Aqueous copper(II) ions are pale blue because they are present as $[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$.

- With excess aqueous ammonia (a little ammonia first gives a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide, which dissolves in excess): $[\mathrm{Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}}]^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 4\mathrm{NH_{3}}\mathrm{(aq)} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Cu(NH_{3})_{4}(H_{2}O)_{2}}]^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 4\mathrm{H_{2}O}\mathrm{(l)}$ The new complex is deep blue.
- With concentrated hydrochloric acid: $[\mathrm{Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}}]^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 4\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\mathrm{(aq)} \rightarrow [\mathrm{CuCl_{4}}]^{2-}\mathrm{(aq)} + 6\mathrm{H_{2}O}\mathrm{(l)}$ The tetrachloridocuprate(II) ion is yellow-green and tetrahedral; the change from 6 to 4 ligands happens because chloride ions are larger than water molecules.
- Silver chloride dissolves in aqueous ammonia: $\mathrm{AgCl}\mathrm{(s)} + 2\mathrm{NH_{3}}\mathrm{(aq)} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Ag(NH_{3})_{2}}]^{+}\mathrm{(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-}\mathrm{(aq)}$

**Origin of colour.** The ligands split the five d orbitals of the metal ion into two groups with a small energy gap. An electron absorbs a part of visible light to jump to the higher group, and the colour seen is the light that remains. A different ligand changes the gap and therefore the colour. Ions with no d electrons (Sc$^{3+}$) or a full d subshell (Zn$^{2+}$, Cu$^{+}$) cannot make such a jump, so their compounds are white or colourless.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, $\mathrm{CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O}$, of mass $2.50\ \mathrm{g}$ is dissolved in water. Excess aqueous ammonia is then added and the solution turns deep blue. ($A_r$: Cu = 63.5, S = 32.1, O = 16.0, H = 1.0.)

(a) Write an equation for the formation of the complex ion that causes the deep blue colour, starting from the hydrated copper(II) ion.

(b) State its coordination number and the oxidation state of copper, and name it.

(c) Calculate the minimum volume of $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ aqueous ammonia needed to convert all the copper(II) ions into this complex.

etapes.action: Identify the reaction as ligand exchange.
etapes.justification: The pale blue solution contains $[\mathrm{Cu(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$. Ammonia is a stronger ligand than water and replaces four of the six water ligands.

etapes.action: Count the donor atoms and find the oxidation state of copper.
etapes.justification: The coordination number is the number of dative bonds; the ligands NH3 and H2O are neutral, so the charge on the complex is the oxidation state of copper.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Coordination number $= 4 + 2 = 6$ (four N atoms and two O atoms). Oxidation state: $x + 0 = +2$, so copper is $+2$.

etapes.justification: Ligands are listed alphabetically, ammine before aqua, with the prefixes tetra and di; the complex is a cation so the metal keeps its name.

etapes.action: Calculate the amount of copper(II) ions.
etapes.justification: One formula unit of the hydrated salt contains one $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ion, so $n(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}) = n(\text{salt})$. First find the relative formula mass.

etapes.action: Use the stoichiometry and the concentration.
etapes.justification: Four ammonia molecules are needed for each copper(II) ion, and volume = amount / concentration.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The deep blue ion is $[\mathrm{Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2}]^{2+}$, with coordination number 6 and copper in the +2 state, and at least $40.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ ammonia is needed; in practice an excess is added to push the exchange to completion.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving the coordination number of $[\mathrm{Ni(en)_3}]^{2+}$ as 3 because there are three ligands.
items.pourquoi_faux: The coordination number counts the dative bonds formed with the metal ion, that is, the donor atoms, not the ligands. Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate.
items.correction_markdown: Each en donates from two nitrogen atoms: $3 \times 2 = 6$, so the coordination number is 6.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that cobalt has oxidation state $-2$ in $[\mathrm{CoCl_4}]^{2-}$ because the complex ion has a charge of 2-.
items.pourquoi_faux: The charge on the complex is the sum of the metal oxidation state and the ligand charges, not the oxidation state of the metal itself.
items.correction_markdown: $x + 4(-1) = -2$, so $x = +2$: cobalt is in the +2 state.

items.pourquoi_faux: A complex that is an anion takes the ending -ate on the metal name, and iron uses its Latin stem in this case.
items.correction_markdown: $x + 6(-1) = -4$ gives $x = +2$; the name is hexacyanidoferrate(II) ion.

items.pourquoi_faux: Ligands are put in alphabetical order of the ligand names; the numerical prefixes di and tetra are ignored when ordering.
items.correction_markdown: Ammine comes before chlorido, so the name is tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) ion.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that a ligand must be a negative ion, so that NH3 and H2O cannot be ligands.
items.pourquoi_faux: What a ligand needs is a lone pair to donate to the metal ion; its overall charge is irrelevant. Neutral molecules such as NH3 and H2O are very common ligands.
items.correction_markdown: Ligands may be neutral (NH3, H2O, en) or negative (Cl-, CN-, OH-, C2O4 2-); each has one or more lone pairs.

items.enonce_markdown: Iron(III) forms a complex with six cyanide ions. (a) Write the formula of the complex ion, including its charge. (b) State its coordination number. (c) Name it.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Charge $= +3 + 6(-1) = -3$, so the formula is $[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{3-}$.

(b) Each cyanide ion is monodentate, so the coordination number is **6**.

(c) The complex is an anion, so the ending is -ate and the Latin stem ferr- is used: **hexacyanidoferrate(III) ion**.

items.enonce_markdown: The cobalt(III) ion forms a complex with three ethanedioate ions, $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$. Each ethanedioate ion is bidentate. (a) Work out the charge on the complex ion and write its formula. (b) State the coordination number and the shape. (c) Name the complex.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Charge $= +3 + 3(-2) = -3$. The formula is $[\mathrm{Co(C_2O_4)_3}]^{3-}$.

(b) Three bidentate ligands give $3 \times 2 =$ **6** dative bonds, so the coordination number is 6 and the shape is **octahedral**.

(c) The complex is an anion: **tris(ethanedioato)cobaltate(III) ion** (also written trisoxalatocobaltate(III)).

items.enonce_markdown:
Aqueous nickel(II) ions exist as $[\mathrm{Ni(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$. When ethane-1,2-diamine (en) is added the complex $[\mathrm{Ni(en)_3}]^{2+}$ forms.

(a) Write a balanced equation for the exchange.

(b) Explain why this reaction goes almost to completion although six Ni-O bonds are replaced by six Ni-N bonds of similar strength.

(c) Calculate the minimum volume of $0.500\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ en needed to convert all the nickel(II) ions in $20.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ nickel(II) solution.

(d) Name $[\mathrm{Ni(en)_3}]^{2+}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $[\mathrm{Ni(H_{2}O)_{6}}]^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 3\mathrm{en}\mathrm{(aq)} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Ni(en)_3}]^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 6\mathrm{H_{2}O}\mathrm{(l)}$

(b) The reaction replaces 4 particles (1 complex ion and 3 en molecules) by 7 particles (1 complex ion and 6 water molecules). The number of free particles increases, so the entropy of the system increases and the exchange is strongly favoured (the chelate effect).

(c) $n(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}) = 0.0200 \times 0.100 = 2.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$; $n(\mathrm{en}) = 3 \times 2.00\times10^{-3} = 6.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$; $V = \dfrac{6.00\times10^{-3}}{0.500} = 0.0120\ \mathrm{dm^3} =$ **12.0 cm3**.

(d) Oxidation state $+2$ (en is neutral), cation: **tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)nickel(II) ion**.

items_markdown: A complex ion has a central metal ion bonded to ligands by dative bonds; each ligand has at least one lone pair, and the metal ion has low-lying empty orbitals. A charge above +2 is not required.
Coordination number = number of donor atoms bonded to the metal; a bidentate ligand such as en or ethanedioate counts twice.
Charge on the complex = oxidation state of the metal + sum of the ligand charges; use it to find the oxidation state.
Name: ligands in alphabetical order with prefixes di, tri, tetra (bis, tris for complicated names), then the metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals; anions end in -ate.
Ligand exchange changes the colour (for example pale blue to deep blue with ammonia); chelating ligands give very stable complexes because the entropy increases.
